question: How is a qualified electronic signature validated?
answer_text:
A qualified electronic signature is validated by a process that must confirm all of the following conditions (E Art. 32):
- The certificate supporting the signature was, at the time of signing, a qualified certificate for electronic signature complying with Annex I (E Art. 32.1(a)).  
- The qualified certificate was issued by a qualified trust service provider and was valid at the time of signing (E Art. 32.1(b)).  
- The signature validation data corresponds to the data provided to the relying party (E Art. 32.1(c)).  
- The unique set of data representing the signatory in the certificate is correctly provided to the relying party (E Art. 32.1(d)).  
- If a pseudonym was used at the time of signing, the use of any pseudonym is clearly indicated to the relying party (E Art. 32.1(e)).  
- The electronic signature was created by a qualified electronic signature creation device (E Art. 32.1(f)).  
- The integrity of the signed data has not been compromised (E Art. 32.1(g)).  
- The requirements of Article 26 were met at the time of signing (E Art. 32.1(h); E Art. 26).  

Article 26 requires an advanced electronic signature to be uniquely linked to the signatory; capable of identifying the signatory; created using signature-creation data the signatory can use under his sole control with a high level of confidence; and linked to the signed data so any subsequent change is detectable (E Art. 26).

Additional validation-system and service requirements:
- The system used for validation must provide the relying party with the correct result and allow the relying party to detect any security-relevant issues (E Art. 32.2).  
- A qualified validation service may only be provided by a qualified trust service provider that performs validation in compliance with Article 32(1) and allows relying parties to receive the validation result in an automated, reliable and efficient manner, bearing the provider’s advanced electronic signature or seal (E Art. 33.1).  
- Compliance with reference standards established by the Commission creates a presumption that the requirements of Article 32(1) (and of the qualified validation service requirements) are met (E Art. 32.3; E Art. 33.2).

question: Why is there a specific discipline for the notification of security breaches?
answer_text:
- To ensure concerned parties receive adequate information when security or integrity is lost (E Rec. 38).

question: What is the applicable law to the trust service provider which provides its trusted services in a Member State different from the one where it is established?
answer_text:
- There shall be no restriction on the provision of trust services in the territory of a Member State by a trust service provider established in another Member State for reasons that fall within the fields covered by this Regulation (E Art. 4.1).

- Products and trust services that comply with this Regulation shall be permitted to circulate freely in the internal market (E Art. 4.2).

- Member States may maintain or introduce national provisions, in conformity with Union law, only insofar as those trust services are not fully harmonised by this Regulation; trust services that comply with the Regulation should circulate freely (E Rec. 24).

question: When do electronic signatures qualify as "advanced electronic signatures"?
answer_text:
An electronic signature is an "advanced electronic signature" when it meets all of the following requirements (E Art. 26):
- it is uniquely linked to the signatory; (E Art. 26)  
- it is capable of identifying the signatory; (E Art. 26)  
- it is created using electronic signature creation data that the signatory can, with a high level of confidence, use under his sole control; (E Art. 26)  
- it is linked to the data signed therewith in such a way that any subsequent change in the data is detectable. (E Art. 26)

Compliance with those requirements is presumed when the advanced electronic signature meets reference standards established by the Commission by implementing acts (E Art. 27.4).

question: When is it mandatory to carry out a Data Protection Impact Assessment?
answer_text:
- General rule: A data protection impact assessment (DPIA) is mandatory where a type of processing, in particular using new technologies and taking into account the nature, scope, context and purposes of the processing, is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons; the DPIA must be carried out prior to the processing (G Art. 35.1; G Rec. 90).

- Specific cases listed as requiring a DPIA (G Art. 35.3):
  - (a) a systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects relating to natural persons based on automated processing, including profiling, on which decisions are based that produce legal effects concerning the natural person or similarly significantly affect them (G Art. 35.3(a));
  - (b) processing on a large scale of special categories of data referred to in Article 9 or data relating to criminal convictions and offences (G Art. 35.3(b));
  - (c) systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area on a large scale (G Art. 35.3(c)).

- Examples and further clarification: large‑scale processing (regional, national or supranational), use of new technologies on a large scale, profiling for decision‑making, processing of special categories/biometric/criminal‑conviction data, and large‑scale monitoring of publicly accessible areas are the kinds of operations that are likely to result in a high risk and therefore require a DPIA (G Rec. 91).

- Implementation detail: supervisory authorities shall establish and publish lists of processing operations that are subject to the DPIA requirement (and may publish lists of operations for which no DPIA is required) (G Art. 35.4–35.5).

question: What are the possible security measures that can be adopted to mitigate the risks related to personal data processing?
answer_text:
Possible security measures (as given in the context)

- Pseudonymisation of personal data (G Art. 32.1(a); G Art. 25.1; G Rec. 78).  
- Encryption of personal data (G Art. 32.1(a); G Rec. 83).  
- Measures to ensure ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of processing systems and services (G Art. 32.1(b)).  
- Ability to restore availability and access to personal data in a timely manner after a physical or technical incident (G Art. 32.1(c)).  
- A process for regularly testing, assessing and evaluating the effectiveness of technical and organisational measures (G Art. 32.1(d)).  
- Data-protection-by-design and by-default measures: minimising processing, integrating safeguards into processing, pseudonymising as soon as possible, and ensuring that by default only personal data necessary for each specific purpose are processed (G Art. 25.1; G Art. 25.2; G Rec. 78).  
- Internal policies and organisational measures to enable transparency about processing, enable data subjects to monitor processing, and enable controllers to create and improve security features (G Rec. 78).  
- Organisational/contractual steps to ensure any person acting under the controller’s or processor’s authority processes personal data only on the controller’s instructions (G Art. 32 para. 4).  
- Risk evaluation and adoption of measures taking account of the state of the art and costs of implementation (G Rec. 83; G Art. 32.1).

question: What are the applicable rules to the processing of personal data for archiving purposes in the public interest, for scientific or historical research purposes or for statistical purposes?
answer_text:

(G Art. 5.1(a)-(f); G Art. 5.2)

- Safeguards may include pseudonymisation, provided the purposes can be fulfilled in that manner, and where the purposes can be fulfilled by processing that does not permit (or no longer permits) identification, they shall be fulfilled in that manner. (G Art. 89.1; G Rec. 156)

- Controllers remain responsible for, and must be able to demonstrate, compliance with the applicable principles and safeguards. (G Art. 5.2; G Art. 89.1)

  - For scientific or historical research purposes or statistical purposes: possible derogations from the rights in Articles 15, 16, 18 and 21. (G Art. 89.2)
  - For archiving purposes in the public interest: possible derogations from the rights in Articles 15, 16, 18, 19, 20 and 21. (G Art. 89.3; G Rec. 156)

- The Regulation applies to processing for archiving purposes in the public interest, except that it does not apply to deceased persons; Member States may authorise further processing for specific archiving aims (examples given in recital). (G Rec. 158)

question: What are the applicable rules to the processing of personal data for archiving purposes in the public interest, for scientific or historical research purposes or for statistical purposes?
answer_text:
- General safeguard requirement: Processing for archiving in the public interest, scientific or historical research, or statistical purposes must be subject to appropriate safeguards, including technical and organisational measures to ensure data minimisation (Art. 89.1; G Rec. 156).

- Measures and methods:
  - Measures may include pseudonymisation and, where those purposes can be fulfilled by further processing that does not permit or no longer permits identification, they shall be fulfilled in that manner (Art. 89.1; G Rec. 156).
  - Controllers must assess feasibility of fulfilling those purposes by processing non‑identifying data and implement measures aimed at minimising processing in line with proportionality and necessity (G Rec. 156).

- Derogations from data‑subject rights:
  - For scientific or historical research or statistical purposes, Union or Member State law may provide derogations from the rights in Articles 15, 16, 18 and 21, subject to the conditions and safeguards of Art. 89.1 (G Art. 89.2).
  - For archiving purposes in the public interest, Union or Member State law may provide derogations from the rights in Articles 15, 16, 18, 19, 20 and 21, subject to the conditions and safeguards of Art. 89.1 (G Art. 89.3).
  - Member States may in particular provide, under conditions and safeguards, specifications and derogations regarding information requirements and rights such as rectification, erasure/to be forgotten, restriction of processing, data portability and the right to object when processing for these purposes (G Rec. 156).

- Applicability and scope:
  - This Regulation applies to processing for archiving, historical research (including genealogical research) and statistical purposes; it does not apply to deceased persons (G Rec. 158; G Rec. 160).
  - Member States may authorise further processing for archiving purposes to address matters such as political behaviour under former totalitarian regimes, genocide, crimes against humanity or war crimes (G Rec. 158).

- Statistical‑specific rules:
  - For statistical purposes, Union or Member State law should determine statistical content, control of access, specifications for processing and measures to safeguard data‑subject rights and statistical confidentiality; statistical results are aggregate (not personal data) and must not be used to support measures or decisions regarding any particular natural person (G Rec. 162).

- Relationship to other principles and processing operations:
  - Further processing for these purposes is to be considered compatible with the original purposes of collection; controllers should assess compatibility taking into account factors such as links between purposes, context, nature of the data, consequences for data subjects and existence of safeguards, and must ensure information to data subjects and the right to object (G Rec. 50).
  - Personal data may be stored for longer periods insofar as they will be processed solely for archiving, scientific/historical research or statistical purposes in accordance with Article 89 (G Art. 5.1(f)).

- Special categories of data:
  - Derogations for processing special categories (e.g. health data) for archiving, research or statistical purposes may be allowed under Union or Member State law but are subject to suitable safeguards and may be further regulated by Member States (G Rec. 52; G Rec. 53; G Art. 9.2(j)).

- Other compliance note:
  - Processing for scientific purposes should also comply with other relevant legislation where applicable (for example on clinical trials) (G Rec. 156).

question: What are the rules applicable to biometric data?
answer_text:
- Biometric data are treated as a special category of personal data: Art. 9(1) includes "biometric data for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person" among the prohibited categories (G Art. 9).

- General rule: processing of such biometric data is prohibited, except where one of the specific derogations in Article 9(2) applies. - Photographs are not automatically special‑category biometric data: a photograph constitutes biometric data only when it is "processed through a specific technical means allowing the unique identification or authentication of a natural person" (G Rec. 51).

- Member States may impose additional conditions or limitations on processing biometric data: Art. 9(4) and Recital 53 allow Member States to maintain or introduce further conditions, including limitations, regarding biometric (and genetic or health) data (G Art. 9.4; G Rec. 53).

- Recital 51 also recalls that, in addition to any specific requirements for processing special categories, the general principles and other rules of the Regulation apply to such processing (G Rec. 51).

question: How should a data processing record be drafted?
answer_text:

  - Each processor and, where applicable, the processor's representative (G Art. 30.2).

  - the name and contact details of the controller and, where applicable, the joint controller, the controller's representative and the data protection officer; (G Art. 30.1(a))
  - the purposes of the processing; (G Art. 30.1(b))
  - a description of the categories of data subjects and of the categories of personal data; (G Art. 30.1(c))
  - the categories of recipients to whom the personal data have been or will be disclosed including recipients in third countries or international organisations; (G Art. 30.1(d))
  - where applicable, transfers of personal data to a third country or an international organisation, including the identification of that third country or international organisation and, where possible, the envisaged time limits for erasure of the different categories of data; (G Art. 30.1(e))
  - where possible, a general description of the technical and organisational security measures referred to in Article 32. (G Art. 30.1(g))

- Required content of a processor's record (must contain the following) (G Art. 30.2):
  - the name and contact details of the processor or processors and of each controller on behalf of which the processor is acting, and, where applicable, of the controller's or the processor's representative, and the data protection officer; (G Art. 30.2(a))
  - the categories of processing carried out on behalf of each controller; (G Art. 30.2(b))

question: How should a data processing record be drafted?
answer_text:
A data‑processing record must be maintained and drafted as follows.

Who must keep records
- Each controller (and, where applicable, the controller’s representative) must maintain a record of processing activities under its responsibility (G Art. 30.1).
- Each processor (and, where applicable, the processor’s representative) must maintain a record of all categories of processing activities carried out on behalf of a controller (G Art. 30.2).

Mandatory contents for controllers’ records (G Art. 30.1)
- Name and contact details of the controller and, where applicable, the joint controller, the controller’s representative and the data protection officer (G Art. 30.1(a)).
- The purposes of the processing (G Art. 30.1(b)).
- A description of the categories of data subjects and of the categories of personal data (G Art. 30.1(c)).
- The categories of recipients to whom the personal data have been or will be disclosed, including recipients in third countries or international organisations (G Art. 30.1(d)).
- Where applicable, transfers of personal data to a third country or an international organisation, including the identification of that third country or international organisation (G Art. 30.1(e)).
- Where possible, envisaged time limits for erasure of the different categories of data (G Art. 30.1(e)).
- Where possible, a general description of the technical and organisational security measures referred to in Article 32 (G Art. 30.1(g); G Art. 32).

Mandatory contents for processors’ records (G Art. 30.2)
- Name and contact details of the processor(s) and of each controller on behalf of which the processor is acting, and, where applicable, of the controller’s or the processor’s representative, and the data protection officer (G Art. 30.2(a)).
- The categories of processing carried out on behalf of each controller (G Art. 30.2(b)).
- Where applicable, transfers of personal data to a third country or an international organisation, including the identification of that third country or international organisation (G Art. 30.2(c)).
- Where possible, a general description of the technical and organisational security measures referred to in Article 32 (G Art. 30.2(d); G Art. 32).

Additional drafting and documentary requirements
- Records serve to demonstrate compliance and should be made available to the supervisory authority on request (G Rec. 82).
- Records and related communications should be transparent, using clear and plain language about identity of the controller and purposes of processing (G Rec. 39).
- Where transfers rely on derogations or safeguards under Article 49, the controller or processor must document the assessment and the suitable safeguards (G Art. 49.6).

Practical implication to include in the drafting
- Describe, as far as possible, the technical and organisational measures relevant to security (e.g. measures falling under Article 32) and, where applicable, time limits for erasure or review of stored categories of data (G Art. 30.1(g); G Art. 30.1(e); G Art. 32; G Rec. 39).

question: What data processing poses significant risks to the fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons?
answer_text:
Processing that poses significant risks to fundamental rights and freedoms includes:

- Processing of particularly sensitive (special categories) personal data (e.g. racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, trade‑union membership, genetic data, biometric data for unique identification, health data, data concerning sex life or sexual orientation) (G Art. 9; G Rec. 51).  
- Processing likely to cause discrimination, identity theft or fraud, financial loss, reputational damage, loss of confidentiality (including data protected by professional secrecy), unauthorised reversal of pseudonymisation, or other significant economic or social disadvantage (G Rec. 75).  
- Processing that may deprive data subjects of rights and freedoms or prevent them exercising control over their personal data (G Rec. 75).  
- Systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects based on automated processing, including profiling, where decisions produce legal effects or similarly significantly affect the person (e.g. automated credit refusals, e‑recruiting) (G Art. 35.3(a); G Rec. 71).  
- Processing of personal aspects to analyse or predict performance at work, economic situation, health, preferences/interests, reliability or behaviour, location or movements to create/use personal profiles (G Rec. 75; G Rec. 71).  
- Processing of personal data of vulnerable natural persons, in particular children (G Rec. 75).  
- Processing involving large amounts of personal data affecting a large number of data subjects, including large‑scale processing of special categories or systematic monitoring of publicly accessible areas on a large scale (G Rec. 75; G Art. 35.3(b)–(c)).

question: What elements should be included in a Code of Conduct?
answer_text:
A code of conduct should specify the matters listed in Article 40(2), namely (inter alia):
- fair and transparent processing (G Art. 40.2(a))  
- the legitimate interests pursued by controllers in specific contexts (G Art. 40.2(b))  
- the collection of personal data (G Art. 40.2(c))  
- the pseudonymisation of personal data (G Art. 40.2(d))  
- the information provided to the public and to data subjects (G Art. 40.2(e))  
- the exercise of the rights of data subjects (G Art. 40.2(f))  
- the information provided to, and the protection of, children, and how parental consent is to be obtained (G Art. 40.2(g))  
- the measures and procedures referred to in Articles 24 and 25 and the measures to ensure security of processing referred to in Article 32 (G Art. 40.2(h))  
- the notification of personal data breaches to supervisory authorities and the communication of such breaches to data subjects (G Art. 40.2(i))  
- the transfer of personal data to third countries or international organisations (G Art. 40.2(j))  
- out‑of‑court proceedings and other dispute‑resolution procedures between controllers and data subjects (without prejudice to rights under Articles 77 and 79) (G Art. 40.2(k))

Additional requirements when drawing up or amending a code:
- take account of the specific features of processing sectors and the needs of micro, small and medium‑sized enterprises (G Art. 40.1)  
- consult relevant stakeholders, including data subjects where feasible, and have regard to submissions and views received (G Rec. 99).

question: What are the obligations of the data controller when the legal basis for the data processing is the consent of the data subject?
answer_text:
- Demonstrate that the data subject has consented to the processing (Art. 7.1; Rec. 42).

- If consent is given in a written declaration that also concerns other matters:
  - present the request for consent in a manner clearly distinguishable from the other matters, in an intelligible and easily accessible form, using clear and plain language (Art. 7.2; Rec. 42);
  - any part of such a declaration that infringes the Regulation is not binding (Art. 7.2).

- Ensure consent is informed by making the data subject aware at least of the identity of the controller and the purposes of the processing (Rec. 42).

- Ensure consent is freely given:
  - take utmost account of whether performance of a contract or provision of a service is conditional on consent to processing that is not necessary for that contract or service (Art. 7.4);
  - do not rely on consent where the data subject has no genuine or free choice or is unable to refuse or withdraw consent without detriment (Rec. 42).

- Inform the data subject, prior to giving consent, that they have the right to withdraw consent at any time; make withdrawal as easy as giving consent; withdrawal does not affect the lawfulness of processing based on consent before its withdrawal (Art. 7.3; Rec. 42).

- When using pre-formulated (controller‑provided) declarations, ensure they are intelligible, easily accessible, use clear and plain language and do not contain unfair terms (Rec. 42).

question: What are the obligations of the data controller when the legal basis for the data processing is the consent of the data subject?
answer_text:
When processing is based on the data subject's consent, the controller must:

- Be able to demonstrate that the data subject has consented to the processing. (G Art.7.1; G Rec.42)

- If consent is given in a written declaration that also concerns other matters, present the request for consent in a way that is clearly distinguishable from the other matters, intelligible and easily accessible, using clear and plain language; any part of such a declaration that infringes the Regulation is not binding. - Give the data subject the right to withdraw consent at any time; withdrawal must be as easy as giving consent and does not affect the lawfulness of processing carried out on the basis of consent before its withdrawal. (G Art.7.3)

- When assessing whether consent is freely given, take utmost account of, inter alia, whether performance of a contract (including provision of a service) is made conditional on consent to processing that is not necessary for performance of that contract; ensure consent is a genuine, free choice and that the data subject can refuse or withdraw without detriment. (G Art.7.4; G Rec.42)

- Ensure any controller‑preformulated declaration of consent is intelligible, easily accessible, uses clear and plain language, and does not contain unfair terms; provide safeguards so the data subject is aware of the fact and extent of the consent. (G Rec.42)

question: What are the obligations of the data controller when the legal basis for the data processing is the consent of the data subject?
answer_text:
- Legal basis: consent is one of the lawful bases for processing (G Art. 6.1(a)).  
- Burden of proof: the controller must be able to demonstrate that the data subject has consented (G Art. 7.1; G Rec. 42).  
- Form and evidencing of consent:
  - Consent must be given by a clear affirmative act establishing a freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication of agreement (G Rec. 32).  
  - Silence, pre‑ticked boxes or inactivity do not constitute consent (G Rec. 32).  
  - Where consent is given in the context of a written declaration on another matter, safeguards must ensure the data subject is aware that and to what extent consent is given (G Rec. 42).  
  - A pre‑formulated declaration of consent must be intelligible and easily accessible, using clear and plain language and must not contain unfair terms (G Rec. 42).  
- Content of the information supporting consent: the data subject should be aware at least of the identity of the controller and the purposes of the processing (G Rec. 42).  
- Scope and granularity:
  - Consent should cover all processing activities carried out for the same purpose(s); if processing has multiple purposes, consent must be given for all of them (G Rec. 32).  
  - Separate consent should be possible for different processing operations where appropriate; consent is presumed not freely given if it does not allow such separate consent when appropriate (G Rec. 43).  
- Freely given requirement:
  - Consent must be freely given; it is not freely given where there is a clear imbalance between data subject and controller (in particular where the controller is a public authority) or where the data subject has no genuine or free choice (G Rec. 43; G Rec. 42).  
  - Consent is not freely given if the performance of a contract or provision of a service is made conditional on consent that is not necessary for that performance (G Rec. 43).  
- Electronic requests: if consent is requested by electronic means, the request must be clear, concise and not unnecessarily disruptive to the use of the service (G Rec. 32).  
- Withdrawal: consent should not be regarded as freely given if the data subject is unable to refuse or withdraw consent without detriment — the controller must not place the data subject in that position (G Rec. 42).

question: Which law is applicable to a non-contractual obligation?
answer_text:
- Autonomous concept: for the purposes of the Regulation, a "non‑contractual obligation" is an autonomous concept (Rec. 11).

- Pre‑contractual dealings (culpa in contrahendo): governed by the law that applies to the contract or would have applied if the contract had been entered into (Art. 12.1). Where that law cannot be determined, the applicable law is (Art. 12.2):  
  - (a) the law of the country in which the damage occurs; or  
  - (b) if the parties have their habitual residence in the same country when the event giving rise to the damage occurs, the law of that country; or  
  - (c) if the obligation is manifestly more closely connected with another country, the law of that other country (Art. 12.2).

- Acts performed without due authority in connection with another's affairs (negotiorum gestio): if the non‑contractual obligation concerns a relationship between the parties (e.g. contractual or tortious) that is closely connected, it is governed by the law governing that relationship (Art. 11.1). Where that law cannot be determined, the applicable law is, in order (Art. 11.2–4):  
  - the law of the country of the parties' common habitual residence at the relevant time (Art. 11.2); or  
  - the law of the country in which the act was performed (Art. 11.3); or  
  - if manifestly more closely connected with another country, the law of that other country (Art. 11.4).

- Unfair competition and restrictions of competition: the law of the country where competitive relations or the collective interests of consumers are, or are likely to be, affected (Art. 6.1). Special rules apply where only a specific competitor is affected (Art. 6.2) and for restrictions of competition and multi‑State markets (Art. 6.3). Article 6.4 provides that the law chosen under Article 6 may not be derogated from by agreement pursuant to Article 14 (Art. 6.4).

- Burden of proof and presumptions: the law governing the non‑contractual obligation applies to the extent it contains rules that raise presumptions of law or determine the burden of proof; modes of proof follow Art. 22 (Art. 22.1–2).

question: What factors should be taken into account for conferring the jurisdiction to determine disputes under a consumer contract?
answer_text:
- The nature of the contract: whether it is (a) a sale of goods on instalment credit terms, (b) a loan repayable by instalments or other credit made to finance the sale of goods, or (c) another contract concluded with a trader who pursues commercial/professional activities in the consumer’s Member State or directs such activities to that State (and the contract falls within those activities) (B Art. 17.1(a)–(c)).

- The domicile/place of parties: a consumer may sue either in the courts of the Member State where the other party is domiciled or in the courts for the place where the consumer is domiciled; conversely, proceedings may be brought against a consumer only in the courts of the Member State where the consumer is domiciled (B Art. 18.1–2).

- Whether the trader has a branch, agency or other establishment in a Member State: a trader not domiciled in a Member State but having such an establishment there is deemed domiciled in that Member State for disputes arising out of the operations of that establishment (B Art. 17.2).

- Whether the trader’s activity is “directed” to the consumer’s Member State and the contract was concluded within the framework of those activities; for distance/Internet sales, mere accessibility of a website is not sufficient — relevant factors include whether the site solicits distance contracts and whether a contract has actually been concluded at a distance (RI Rec. 24).

- Exceptions and limits: the consumer-jurisdiction rules do not apply to certain transport contracts (except combined travel/accommodation) (B Art. 17.3), and the Section’s rules may be departed from only in the limited cases listed by agreement (B Art. 19.1).

- Where the defendant is not domiciled in a Member State, jurisdiction of each Member State’s courts is determined by the law of that Member State, subject to the consumer-protection rule (B Art. 6.1).
